title: Calculus of the Hyperbolic Functions
lead: The hyperbolic functions, built from $e^{x}$ and $e^{-x},$ have derivatives and integrals that echo the trigonometric ones with some changes of sign; their inverses, written with logarithms, give antiderivatives of $1/\sqrt{1+u^{2}},$ $1/\sqrt{u^{2}-1}$ and $1/(1-u^{2}).$ A cable hanging under its own weight is a catenary, $y=a\cosh(x/a),$ whose length is an integral the identities make easy.
objectives: Apply the formulas for derivatives and integrals of the hyperbolic functions.
Apply the formulas for the derivatives of the inverse hyperbolic functions and their associated integrals.
Describe the common applied conditions of a catenary curve.
summary_html:
• Hyperbolic functions are defined in terms of exponential functions.
  • Term-by-term differentiation yields differentiation formulas for the hyperbolic functions. These differentiation formulas give rise, in turn, to integration formulas.
  • With appropriate range restrictions, the hyperbolic functions all have inverses.
  • Implicit differentiation yields differentiation formulas for the inverse hyperbolic functions, which in turn give rise to integration formulas.
  • The most common physical applications of hyperbolic functions are calculations involving catenaries.

exercises.prompt: [T] Find expressions for $\text{cosh}\;x+\text{sinh}\;x$ and $\text{cosh}\;x-\text{sinh}\;x.$ Use a calculator to graph these functions and ensure your expression is correct.
Show that $\text{cosh}(x)$ and $\text{sinh}(x)$ satisfy $y^{''}=y.$

answer.solution: From the definitions, $(\cosh x)'=\frac{e^{x}-e^{-x}}{2}=\sinh x$ and $(\sinh x)'=\frac{e^{x}+e^{-x}}{2}=\cosh x.$ So $(\cosh x)''=(\sinh x)'=\cosh x$ and $(\sinh x)''=(\cosh x)'=\sinh x:$ each satisfies $y''=y.$

exercises.prompt: Use the quotient rule to verify that $\text{tanh}(x)'={\text{sech}}^{2}(x).$

answer.solution: $\tanh x=\frac{\sinh x}{\cosh x},$ so by the quotient rule $(\tanh x)'=\frac{\cosh x\cdot\cosh x-\sinh x\cdot\sinh x}{\cosh^{2}x}=\frac{1}{\cosh^{2}x}=\text{sech}^{2}x,$ since $\cosh^{2}x-\sinh^{2}x=1.$

exercises.prompt: Derive ${\text{cosh}}^{2}(x)+{\text{sinh}}^{2}(x)=\text{cosh}(2x)$ from the definition.
Take the derivative of the previous expression to find an expression for $\text{sinh}(2x).$

answer.solution: Differentiate both sides of $\cosh^{2}x+\sinh^{2}x=\cosh(2x):$ the left gives $2\cosh x\sinh x+2\sinh x\cosh x=4\sinh x\cosh x,$ the right $2\sinh(2x).$ So $\sinh(2x)=2\sinh x\cosh x.$

exercises.prompt: Prove $\text{sinh}(x+y)=\text{sinh}(x)\text{cosh}(y)+\text{cosh}(x)\text{sinh}(y)$ by changing the expression to exponentials.

answer.solution: $\sinh x\cosh y+\cosh x\sinh y=\frac{(e^{x}-e^{-x})(e^{y}+e^{-y})+(e^{x}+e^{-x})(e^{y}-e^{-y})}{4}.$ Expanding, the numerator is $(e^{x+y}+e^{x-y}-e^{-x+y}-e^{-x-y})+(e^{x+y}-e^{x-y}+e^{-x+y}-e^{-x-y})=2e^{x+y}-2e^{-(x+y)},$ so the sum is $\frac{e^{x+y}-e^{-(x+y)}}{2}=\sinh(x+y).$

exercises.prompt: Take the derivative of the previous expression to find an expression for $\text{cosh}(x+y).$

answer.solution: Differentiate $\sinh(x+y)=\sinh x\cosh y+\cosh x\sinh y$ with respect to x, holding y fixed: $\cosh(x+y)=\cosh x\cosh y+\sinh x\sinh y.$

For the following exercises, use the fact that a falling body with friction equal to velocity squared obeys the equation $dv/dt=g-v^{2}.$

Show that $v(t)=\sqrt{g}\;\text{tanh}((\sqrt{g})t)$ satisfies this equation.

answer.solution: With $v(t)=\sqrt{g}\tanh(\sqrt{g}\,t),$ the chain rule gives $\frac{dv}{dt}=\sqrt{g}\cdot\sqrt{g}\,\text{sech}^{2}(\sqrt{g}\,t)=g\,\text{sech}^{2}(\sqrt{g}\,t).$ Since $\text{sech}^{2}u=1-\tanh^{2}u,$ this is $g-g\tanh^{2}(\sqrt{g}\,t)=g-v^{2}.$

exercises.prompt:
For the following exercises, use the fact that a falling body with friction equal to velocity squared obeys the equation $dv/dt=g-v^{2}.$

Derive the previous expression for $v(t)$ by integrating $\frac{dv}{g-v^{2}}=dt.$

answer.solution: For $|v|<\sqrt{g},$ $\int\frac{dv}{g-v^{2}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{g}}\tanh^{-1}\left(\frac{v}{\sqrt{g}}\right)$ (substitute $v=\sqrt{g}\,u$ in $\int\frac{du}{1-u^{2}}=\tanh^{-1}u$). So $\frac{1}{\sqrt{g}}\tanh^{-1}\left(\frac{v}{\sqrt{g}}\right)=t+C,$ and a body starting from rest, $v(0)=0,$ has $C=0.$ Solving, $v(t)=\sqrt{g}\tanh(\sqrt{g}\,t).$

For the following exercises, use this scenario: A cable hanging under its own weight has a slope $S=dy/dx$ that satisfies $dS/dx=c\sqrt{1+S^{2}}.$ The constant $c$ is the ratio of cable density to tension.

Show that $S=\text{sinh}(cx)$ satisfies this equation.

answer.solution: With $S=\sinh(cx),$ $\frac{dS}{dx}=c\cosh(cx),$ and $c\sqrt{1+S^{2}}=c\sqrt{1+\sinh^{2}(cx)}=c\cosh(cx),$ since $\cosh^{2}-\sinh^{2}=1$ and $\cosh>0.$ The two agree.

For the following exercises, solve each problem.

A telephone line is a catenary described by $y=a\;\text{cosh}(x/a).$ Find the ratio of the area under the catenary to its arc length. Does this confirm your answer for the previous question?

answer.solution: Over any interval $[x_{1},x_{2}],$ the area is $\int a\cosh(x/a)\,dx=a^{2}\sinh(x/a)\Big|_{x_{1}}^{x_{2}}$ and the arc length is $\int\sqrt{1+\sinh^{2}(x/a)}\,dx=\int\cosh(x/a)\,dx=a\sinh(x/a)\Big|_{x_{1}}^{x_{2}}.$ Their ratio is a, whatever the interval; for $a=10$ it is 10, as in the previous exercise.

exercises.prompt:
For the following exercises, solve each problem.

Prove the formula for the derivative of $y={\text{sinh}}^{-1}(x)$ by differentiating $x=\text{sinh}(y).$ (Hint: Use hyperbolic trigonometric identities.)

answer.solution: Let $y=\sinh^{-1}x,$ so $x=\sinh y.$ Differentiating implicitly, $1=\cosh y\,\frac{dy}{dx},$ so $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{\cosh y}.$ From $\cosh^{2}y-\sinh^{2}y=1$ and $\cosh y>0,$ $\cosh y=\sqrt{1+\sinh^{2}y}=\sqrt{1+x^{2}}.$ Hence $\frac{d}{dx}\sinh^{-1}x=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+x^{2}}}.$

exercises.prompt:
For the following exercises, solve each problem.

Prove the formula for the derivative of $y={\text{cosh}}^{-1}(x)$ by differentiating $x=\text{cosh}(y).$

(Hint: Use hyperbolic trigonometric identities.)

answer.solution: Let $y=\cosh^{-1}x$ with $x\ge 1$ and $y\ge 0,$ so $x=\cosh y.$ Then $1=\sinh y\,\frac{dy}{dx},$ and for $y\ge 0,$ $\sinh y=\sqrt{\cosh^{2}y-1}=\sqrt{x^{2}-1}.$ So $\frac{d}{dx}\cosh^{-1}x=\frac{1}{\sqrt{x^{2}-1}}$ for $x>1.$

exercises.prompt:
For the following exercises, solve each problem.

Prove the formula for the derivative of $y={\text{sech}}^{-1}(x)$ by differentiating $x=\text{sech}(y).$ (Hint: Use hyperbolic trigonometric identities.)

answer.solution: Let $y=\text{sech}^{-1}x$ with $0<x\le 1$ and $y\ge 0,$ so $x=\text{sech}\,y.$ Differentiating, $1=-\text{sech}\,y\tanh y\,\frac{dy}{dx}.$ With $\tanh^{2}y=1-\text{sech}^{2}y$ and $\tanh y\ge 0$ for $y\ge 0,$ $\tanh y=\sqrt{1-x^{2}}.$ So $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{-1}{x\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}.$

exercises.prompt:
For the following exercises, solve each problem.

Prove that ${(\text{cosh}(x)+\text{sinh}(x))}^{n}=\text{cosh}(nx)+\text{sinh}(nx).$

answer.solution: $\cosh x+\sinh x=\frac{e^{x}+e^{-x}}{2}+\frac{e^{x}-e^{-x}}{2}=e^{x},$ so $(\cosh x+\sinh x)^{n}=e^{nx}=\cosh(nx)+\sinh(nx),$ by the same identity with $nx$ in place of x.

exercises.prompt:
For the following exercises, solve each problem.

Prove the expression for ${\text{sinh}}^{-1}(x).$ Multiply $x=\text{sinh}(y)=(1/2)(e^{y}-e^{-y})$ by $2e^{y}$ and solve for $y.$ Does your expression match the textbook?

answer.solution: Multiply $x=\frac{1}{2}(e^{y}-e^{-y})$ by $2e^{y}:$ $2xe^{y}=e^{2y}-1,$ that is $(e^{y})^{2}-2x\,e^{y}-1=0,$ a quadratic in $e^{y}.$ So $e^{y}=x\pm\sqrt{x^{2}+1},$ and since $e^{y}>0$ while $x-\sqrt{x^{2}+1}<0,$ $e^{y}=x+\sqrt{x^{2}+1}.$ Hence $\sinh^{-1}x=\ln\left(x+\sqrt{x^{2}+1}\right),$ the expression of Section 1.5.

exercises.prompt:
For the following exercises, solve each problem.

Prove the expression for ${\text{cosh}}^{-1}(x).$ Multiply $x=\text{cosh}(y)=(1/2)(e^{y}+e^{-y})$ by $2e^{y}$ and solve for $y.$ Does your expression match the textbook?

answer.solution: Multiply $x=\frac{1}{2}(e^{y}+e^{-y})$ by $2e^{y}:$ $2xe^{y}=e^{2y}+1,$ that is $(e^{y})^{2}-2x\,e^{y}+1=0.$ So $e^{y}=x\pm\sqrt{x^{2}-1}.$ The inverse takes $y\ge 0,$ so $e^{y}\ge 1,$ which is the plus sign (the two roots multiply to 1). Hence $\cosh^{-1}x=\ln\left(x+\sqrt{x^{2}-1}\right)$ for $x\ge 1.$
